title: COINTELPRO and Operation Northwoods
bigQuestion: How were real government secrets exposed, and how can the same test of documents help us judge claims about secrets that are false?

story.title: Eight Citizens in Media
story.kicker: In March 1971, eight people break into a small FBI office in Pennsylvania and mail its files to reporters.
paragraphs: Media, Pennsylvania, is a small town outside Philadelphia. On the night of 8 March 1971, eight people break into the local office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the FBI. There are three women and five men. They include a physics professor and a married couple with young children. None of them are professional burglars.

They call themselves the Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI. Many of them had protested the Vietnam War. They suspect the FBI is spying on peaceful protesters and trying to frighten them into silence. They have no proof. They decide that the only way to get it is to take the files themselves. They know that what they are doing is a crime.

They carry out about 1,000 pages. Over the following weeks, they sort the papers and mail copies to newspapers and to members of Congress. The Justice Department asks newspapers not to print them. The Washington Post decides to publish. Reporter Betty Medsger writes the first story.

One routing slip carries a strange word: COINTELPRO. No one outside the FBI knows what it means. Reporters begin to ask. Within weeks, FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover officially ends the program with that name. The FBI never catches the burglars. In 2014, five of them finally tell their story in Medsger's book, The Burglary.
story.think: The Media burglars broke the law to show that the FBI had broken the rules. How should we judge people who do something illegal to expose a hidden wrong?

lessons.title: The Break-In
lessons.mainIdea: In March 1971, eight citizens stole about 1,000 pages of files from an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, to prove the FBI was spying on protesters.
reading: The *Federal Bureau of Investigation*, or FBI, is the main national police agency of the United States. It investigates federal crimes and threats to national security. By 1971 it had been led for almost fifty years by one man, J. Edgar Hoover. Many Americans admired the FBI. Critics said it had grown too powerful and too secret.

The eight people who broke into the Media office on 8 March 1971 were ordinary citizens with a political goal. They believed the FBI was watching people who opposed the Vietnam War and people working for civil rights. They could not prove it from the outside. So they planned a *burglary*, a break-in to steal property, and chose a small office with little security.

They took about 1,000 pages. When they read them, they found what they had suspected. Some files showed the FBI watching student groups, Black student organizations and peace activists. One file encouraged agents to interview protesters often, so they would feel that there was an FBI agent behind every mailbox.
The burglars mailed copies to reporters and lawmakers. Then they went back to their ordinary lives. The FBI searched for them for years and never charged anyone. They spoke publicly only in 2014.

words.d: the main national police agency of the United States, known as the FBI
breaking into a building to steal something, which is a crime
a person who works to bring about political or social change

look.title: The Media Break-In by the Numbers
look.cite: Betty Medsger, The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover's Secret FBI, Knopf, 2014
look.prompt: Five of the eight came forward in 2014. Why might someone choose to stay unknown for over forty years, and why might others choose to speak?

check.q: What were the Media burglars trying to prove?
choices: That the FBI was spying on peaceful protesters
That the CIA had tested drugs on people
That the Army planned to invade Cuba
That the Media office was poorly run
check.why: They suspected the FBI was watching antiwar and civil rights activists and wanted documents to prove it.

check.q: About how many pages did the burglars take?
check.why: Sources report that about 1,000 pages were taken from the Media office.

check.q: What happened to the burglars?
choices: They were caught within a week
They were tried by the Church Committee
They were pardoned by President Ford
They were never caught, and five spoke publicly in 2014
check.why: The FBI never charged anyone; five came forward in Betty Medsger's 2014 book.

lessons.title: Should the Papers Print It?
lessons.mainIdea: The Washington Post chose to publish stories from the stolen files even though the Justice Department asked it not to.
reading: When the envelopes arrived, editors faced a hard choice. The files were stolen. The Justice Department, which oversees the FBI, asked newspapers not to publish them, warning that doing so could endanger lives and national security. Some papers returned the files or held back.

At The Washington Post, reporter Betty Medsger and her editors read the documents closely. They checked that the files looked real. They weighed the risk of harm against the public's interest in knowing what a government agency was doing. The Post decided that the files showed possible abuse of power and that citizens had a right to know. It published the first story in March 1971.

This is an example of *press freedom* at work. The First Amendment protects the right of newspapers to publish, even information the government wants kept quiet. It also puts a responsibility on journalists to *verify* what they print and to think about harm.
Other papers followed. Once the stories were out, members of Congress and other reporters had a starting point for more questions.

words.d: the right of newspapers and other media to report and publish without government control
to check that something is true or real
the part of the U.S. Constitution that protects freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly and petition

look.title: Two Sides of the Editors' Table
look.text: Editor 1: These papers were stolen. Printing them rewards a crime, and we cannot be sure no one will be hurt. Editor 2: These papers show a government agency may be targeting citizens for their opinions. The public cannot judge that if it never sees the evidence. We will check them carefully and leave out anything that puts a person in danger.
look.prompt: Which argument do you find stronger? What is one step a newspaper could take to respect the concerns on both sides?

check.q: What did the Justice Department ask newspapers to do with the Media files?
check.why: The Justice Department asked papers not to publish, citing risk to lives and security.

check.q: What does 'verify' mean?
choices: To check that something is true or real
check.why: Journalists verify by checking that documents are real before they publish.

check.q: Which newspaper published the first story from the Media files?
check.why: The Washington Post, with reporter Betty Medsger, published first in March 1971.

lessons.title: One Strange Word
lessons.mainIdea: The word COINTELPRO on one Media file led reporters to uncover a secret FBI program, which Hoover ended in April 1971.
reading: Among the Media papers was a routing slip marked COINTELPRO. The word was short for *Counterintelligence Program*. Counterintelligence usually means working against foreign spies. So why would it appear in files about American students and activists?

An NBC News reporter, Carl Stern, decided to find out. He used the Freedom of Information Act to ask the FBI for records about the word. The FBI resisted. Stern went to court. In the end, the FBI had to release papers that showed COINTELPRO was a set of programs aimed at groups inside the United States.

Meanwhile, on 28 April 1971, less than two months after the break-in, Hoover officially ended the programs called COINTELPRO. He said future actions would be handled case by case. Critics pointed out that ending a program's name is not the same as ending its methods.

The full picture came later, when the Church Committee studied the FBI's files in 1975 and 1976. A single word on a slip of paper had opened a *paper trail*. A paper trail is a chain of documents that can be followed from one record to the next.

words.d: work done to detect and stop spying or sabotage by others
short for Counterintelligence Program; the FBI's secret programs (1956–1971) to disrupt groups inside the United States
a chain of documents that can be followed from one record to the next

look.title: Following One Word
look.text: Step 1: A stolen file shows a code word. Step 2: A reporter asks the agency, under the law, what the word means. Step 3: The agency says no. Step 4: A judge orders some records released. Step 5: A Senate committee later reads the full files.
look.prompt: At which step did the secret first become proven, not just suspected? Explain your choice.

check.q: What does COINTELPRO stand for?
check.why: COINTELPRO was short for Counterintelligence Program.

check.q: How did reporter Carl Stern get records about COINTELPRO?
choices: He broke into another FBI office
He was a member of the Church Committee
He used the Freedom of Information Act and went to court
He was given them by J. Edgar Hoover
check.why: Stern filed a FOIA request, the FBI resisted, and a court required release of some records.

check.q: What did Hoover do on 28 April 1971?
choices: He officially ended the programs called COINTELPRO
He testified before the Church Committee
check.why: Hoover officially ended COINTELPRO less than two months after the break-in.

lessons.title: From Watching to Disrupting
lessons.mainIdea: COINTELPRO went beyond investigating crimes: the FBI secretly worked to disrupt and discredit lawful groups and their members.
reading: Investigating a crime means gathering evidence so a court can decide if someone broke the law. COINTELPRO did something different. Its goal was to *disrupt* groups, meaning to break them apart, weaken them and damage their reputations, whether or not their members had committed any crime.

The Church Committee described the methods. Agents sent anonymous letters to stir up quarrels between members or between rival groups. They gave damaging stories to friendly reporters. They tried to get people fired from jobs. They placed *informants*, people who secretly report to the police, inside groups.

Hoover and his agents saw themselves as defending the country. They believed some of these groups were controlled by foreign enemies or were heading toward violence. Some groups did include people who broke laws. But the FBI also targeted people for their ideas and for lawful speech and protest.

The Church Committee concluded that many of these methods would be wrong in a free country even if every target had been violent. The problem was not only who was targeted. It was that a secret agency was acting as judge and punisher without any court.

words.d: to break apart or throw into disorder
a person who secretly gives information about a group to the police or an agency
to damage a person's or group's reputation so others stop trusting them

look.title: The Committee's Judgment on COINTELPRO
look.text: The committee found that COINTELPRO went beyond gathering information to secretly attacking the targets' reputations, relationships and work. It judged that many of these methods would be unacceptable in a democracy even if all of the targets had been involved in violence.
look.cite: Church Committee, Final Report, Book III: Supplementary Detailed Staff Reports on Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans, 1976 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why would the committee say the methods were wrong even if the targets were violent? What should happen instead when someone is suspected of a crime?

check.q: How did COINTELPRO differ from ordinary crime investigation?
choices: It aimed to disrupt groups whether or not members committed crimes
It was carried out by the CIA
It was approved by a court
check.why: Investigation gathers evidence for a court; COINTELPRO tried to break up groups directly, without a court.

check.q: What is an informant?
choices: A person who secretly reports on a group to the police or an agency
A reporter who publishes stolen files
A senator on the Church Committee
check.why: Informants secretly pass information from inside a group to an agency.

check.q: How did Hoover and his agents see their own work?
choices: As a way to win elections
As defending the country from groups they saw as dangerous
As a program ordered by Congress
check.why: The reading says they believed they were protecting the country from groups they saw as controlled by enemies or heading to violence.

lessons.title: Targets Across the Spectrum
lessons.mainIdea: COINTELPRO targeted groups on the left and the right, from the Communist Party to the Ku Klux Klan to civil rights and antiwar groups.
reading: COINTELPRO was not one program but several, started at different times. The first, in 1956, targeted the Communist Party of the United States. Over the next twelve years, the FBI added more. The *political spectrum* is the range of political views, from left to right. COINTELPRO reached across much of it.

In 1961 the FBI added the Socialist Workers Party, a small group on the far left. In 1964 it added white hate groups, including the Ku Klux Klan, which was using terror against Black Americans and civil rights workers. In 1967 it added what it called Black nationalist groups, which swept in major civil rights leaders and organizations. In 1968 it added the New Left, meaning student and antiwar groups.

The Klan program is complicated. The Klan was committing real violence, and many people wanted it stopped. Yet the FBI used the same secret methods against the Klan as against peaceful groups, and it was far more aggressive toward Black-led and antiwar groups.

Most people in every one of these groups were never charged with any crime. Knowing the range helps a reader avoid a simple story. The lesson is not that one side was targeted. It is that secret power, once created, can be pointed at anyone.

words.d: the range of political views, often described from left to right
a white supremacist hate group that has used terror against Black Americans and others
the student and antiwar movements of the 1960s

look.title: When Each COINTELPRO Program Began
look.cite: Church Committee, Final Report, Book III, 1976
look.prompt: What was happening in the country in 1964 through 1968 that might explain why the FBI added three programs in those years?

check.q: Which group was the first target of COINTELPRO in 1956?
choices: The Communist Party of the United States
check.why: The first COINTELPRO program, in 1956, targeted the Communist Party USA.

check.q: What does 'political spectrum' mean?
choices: A secret code used by the FBI
The range of political views from left to right
check.why: The spectrum is the range of views; COINTELPRO reached groups across much of it.

check.q: What main point does the reading draw from the range of COINTELPRO's targets?
choices: The Klan was the FBI's main target
Secret power, once created, can be pointed at anyone
Every target had committed a crime
check.why: The reading says the lesson is that secret power can be turned on anyone, not that one side alone was hit.

lessons.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
lessons.mainIdea: The FBI secretly watched Martin Luther King Jr. for years and tried to discredit him, as the Church Committee documented.
reading: Martin Luther King Jr. led the most famous nonviolent movement in American history. He preached peace and used marches, boycotts and speeches to win civil rights. The FBI treated him as a threat. Hoover disliked him and claimed, without evidence the committee accepted, that he was under Communist influence.

In 1963, Attorney General Robert Kennedy approved FBI *wiretaps*, secret listening devices on phone lines, on King and some of his advisers. The FBI also placed hidden microphones in hotel rooms where King stayed. Agents gathered personal information to use against him.

In 1964, the year King won the Nobel Peace Prize, the FBI mailed him an unsigned letter full of insults and threats, with a recording. King and many historians read the letter as pushing him to take his own life. The Church Committee described this campaign in detail in 1976.

King kept working until he was killed in 1968. His story shows how COINTELPRO-style methods reached even a leader devoted to nonviolence. It also shows *resilience*: the movement continued, and the truth about the FBI's campaign came out through records.

words.d: a secret device or method for listening to someone's phone calls
a way of working for change that refuses to use violence
the ability to keep going and recover after hardship

look.title: Two Ways to Describe a Leader
look.text: How his movement saw him: a minister who asked people to answer hatred with peaceful protest and to hold the nation to its own promises. How the FBI's files described him: a dangerous figure who needed to be watched and brought down.
look.prompt: What evidence in the reading helps you decide which description fits King's actions? What does the gap between the two tell you about the FBI at the time?

check.q: Who approved FBI wiretaps on Martin Luther King Jr. in 1963?
check.why: Attorney General Robert Kennedy approved the wiretaps in 1963.

check.q: What did the FBI mail King in 1964?
choices: A copy of the COINTELPRO files
An unsigned letter full of insults and threats
An invitation to testify before Congress
A thank-you note for his Nobel Prize
check.why: The FBI sent an unsigned, threatening letter that the Church Committee later described.

check.q: What does 'resilience' mean in this lesson?
choices: Keeping going and recovering after hardship
check.why: Resilience is the ability to keep going after hardship, as King and the movement did.

lessons.title: Fred Hampton
lessons.mainIdea: Fred Hampton, a 21-year-old leader of the Illinois Black Panther Party, built community programs and alliances that the FBI saw as a threat.
reading: Fred Hampton grew up in Maywood, a suburb just west of Chicago. As a teenager he was a youth leader in the NAACP, the civil rights organization. In 1968 he joined the Black Panther Party and soon became chairman of its Illinois chapter. He was a powerful speaker who could hold a crowd.

The Black Panther Party was founded in Oakland, California, in 1966. Its members carried guns openly at first and talked about defending Black neighborhoods from police abuse. They also ran *community programs*. In Chicago, the Panthers served free breakfast to children before school and opened a free health clinic.

Hampton also worked to bring different groups together. He reached out to Chicago street organizations and to groups of poor white and Puerto Rican young people, in what was called the Rainbow Coalition. Members saw him as a young leader who could unite people across racial lines.

The FBI saw the same abilities as a danger. Under its COINTELPRO program against Black groups, it watched Hampton closely and placed an informant near him. Seeing both views does not mean they are equal. It means understanding why each side acted as it did.

words.d: a Black political organization founded in Oakland, California, in 1966, known for self-defense and community programs
free services a group runs for its neighbors, such as meals or health care
a group of different organizations that join together for a shared goal

look.title: A Morning Breakfast Program
look.text: Picture a church basement on Chicago's West Side at 7 a.m. Volunteers pour milk and pass out plates of eggs and toast. Children eat before walking to school. On the wall is a Black Panther Party poster. Across town, an FBI file lists the program as part of a group it has marked for disruption.
look.prompt: How might a parent, a Panther member and an FBI agent each describe this scene? What would each one notice first?

check.q: What role did Fred Hampton hold in 1969?
choices: Chairman of the Illinois Black Panther Party
Director of the FBI office in Chicago
check.why: Hampton became chairman of the Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party.

check.q: Which community program did the Chicago Panthers run?
choices: Free breakfast for children before school
check.why: The reading names the free breakfast program and a free health clinic.

check.q: What was the Rainbow Coalition?
choices: An FBI plan to watch Chicago groups
A Senate committee on civil rights
An alliance Hampton built across racial lines
check.why: Hampton reached out to street organizations and poor white and Puerto Rican groups to form the Rainbow Coalition.

lessons.title: The Raid of 4 December 1969
lessons.mainIdea: Before dawn on 4 December 1969, police killed Fred Hampton and Mark Clark in a raid on a West Side apartment, and evidence showed nearly all shots came from police.
reading: Early on 4 December 1969, officers working for Cook County State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan raided an apartment on West Monroe Street on Chicago's West Side. They said they were looking for illegal weapons. Several Panthers were asleep inside, including Fred Hampton and Deborah Johnson, who was expecting their child.

Police fired many shots. Fred Hampton, 21, was killed in his bed. Mark Clark, 22, a Panther leader from Peoria, Illinois, was also killed. Several others were wounded and then arrested. Hanrahan's office said the Panthers had fired first and that the officers had defended themselves.

Evidence soon challenged that account. People from the neighborhood toured the apartment and saw the bullet holes. A federal grand jury in 1970 found that nearly all of the shots had come from police weapons. The charges against the survivors were dropped. Hanrahan and several officers were later charged with blocking justice and were found not guilty in 1972.
Hampton's son, Fred Hampton Jr., was born weeks after the raid. The deaths of two young men are the center of this story. The records matter because they show what happened to them.

words.d: a sudden entry into a place by police or soldiers, often to search or arrest
a group of citizens who review evidence to decide whether someone should be charged with a crime
in Illinois, the elected official who prosecutes crimes for a county

look.title: Two Accounts of One Night
look.text: Account 1, from the State's Attorney's office in December 1969: officers were attacked by gunfire and fired back to defend themselves. Account 2, from the evidence reviewed by a federal grand jury in 1970: nearly all of the shots came from police weapons.
look.prompt: Why would physical evidence, such as where bullets came from, carry more weight than a statement made right after the raid? What makes an account believable?

check.q: Who was killed along with Fred Hampton in the 4 December 1969 raid?
check.why: Mark Clark, 22, a Panther leader from Peoria, was also killed.

check.q: What did a federal grand jury find in 1970?
choices: That the Panthers fired most of the shots
That nearly all the shots came from police weapons
That no raid had taken place
That Hampton had been out of the city
check.why: The grand jury found nearly all shots came from police, which challenged the official account.

check.q: Whose office carried out the raid?
choices: Cook County State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan's office
The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
check.why: The officers worked for Cook County State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan.

lessons.title: The Informant and the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Lawsuits later showed that an FBI informant had given agents a floor plan of Hampton's apartment, and in 1982 three governments paid $1.85 million to settle.
reading: Hampton's family, the survivors and Mark Clark's family sued the officials involved. The case is known as Hampton v. Hanrahan. It took more than a decade. During it, lawyers pried loose FBI documents that the government had fought to keep secret.

The documents showed that William O'Neal, the Chicago chapter's head of security, was a paid FBI informant. He had given his FBI contact a floor plan of the apartment, marking where Hampton slept. The FBI passed the information to the State's Attorney's officers before the raid. Historians still debate how much each official knew and intended.

In 1979, a federal appeals court ruled that there was enough evidence of a cover-up to send the case back for a new trial. In 1982, the case was settled for $1.85 million. The federal government, Cook County and the City of Chicago each paid one-third. A *settlement* is not a verdict. It ends a case without a final finding of guilt.
Chicagoans still remember Hampton. In 1990 the Chicago City Council passed a resolution honoring him. The case shows how courts, not only Congress, can open secret records.

words.d: a case brought to court by a person or group who says they were wronged
an effort to hide the truth about a wrong
an agreement to end a lawsuit, often with a payment, without a final court ruling
a higher court that reviews the decisions of lower courts

look.title: Who Paid the 1982 Settlement
look.cite: Hampton v. Hanrahan settlement, U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois, 1982, as summarized in later accounts
look.prompt: Three different governments each paid one-third. What does that suggest about who was seen as responsible, even without a verdict?

check.q: What did William O'Neal give his FBI contact?
choices: A copy of the COINTELPRO files
A floor plan of Hampton's apartment
A recording of Martin Luther King Jr.
A list of the Media burglars
check.why: Court documents showed O'Neal, a paid informant, supplied a floor plan marking where Hampton slept.

check.q: Why is a settlement different from a verdict?
choices: It ends a case without a final finding of guilt
It is decided by a grand jury
It always sends someone to prison
It can only be reached by the Senate
check.why: A settlement is an agreement to end the case, often with payment, without a final ruling on guilt.

check.q: Who paid the $1.85 million settlement in 1982?
choices: The federal government, Cook County and the City of Chicago
check.why: Each of the three governments paid one-third of the $1.85 million.

lessons.title: A Plan on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: In March 1962, the Joint Chiefs of Staff proposed Operation Northwoods: staged attacks blamed on Cuba to justify a U.S. invasion.
reading: In 1959, Fidel Castro took power in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida, and soon allied with the Soviet Union. In April 1961, a CIA-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs failed. President John F. Kennedy's government kept looking for ways to remove Castro.

On 13 March 1962, General Lyman Lemnitzer, chairman of the *Joint Chiefs of Staff*, the top military leaders, sent a memo to Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. Its title was Justification for U.S. Military Intervention in Cuba. The plan is known as Operation Northwoods.

The memo listed ways to create a *pretext*, a false reason given to hide the real one. It suggested staging fake attacks on the U.S. base at Guantánamo Bay, blowing up a U.S. ship and blaming Cuba, and faking a Cuban attack on an aircraft. The idea was to make the world believe Cuba had attacked first, so an invasion would look justified.

An attack staged to look like the work of an enemy is often called a *false flag* operation. Northwoods matters because it is written proof that top U.S. military leaders once proposed such a plan on paper.

words.d: the group of the top leaders of the U.S. armed forces, who advise the president and defense secretary
a false reason given to hide the real reason for an action
an attack staged to look as if an enemy carried it out
a short written message sent inside an organization; short for memorandum

look.title: What the Northwoods Memo Proposed
look.text: The Joint Chiefs recommended that the defense secretary consider a series of staged incidents that would appear to be Cuban attacks, including actions against the U.S. base at Guantánamo, so that U.S. military intervention in Cuba would seem justified to the world.
look.cite: Joint Chiefs of Staff, memorandum for the Secretary of Defense, Justification for U.S. Military Intervention in Cuba, signed by Gen. L. L. Lemnitzer, 13 March 1962 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: The memo is a proposal, not a report of something done. Which words in the paraphrase show that it describes a plan?

check.q: Who signed the Northwoods memo on 13 March 1962?
check.why: General Lemnitzer, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, signed and sent it to McNamara.

check.q: What is a pretext?
choices: A false reason given to hide the real one
check.why: A pretext is a cover reason; Northwoods proposed staged incidents as a pretext for invasion.

check.q: What did Operation Northwoods propose?
choices: Staged attacks blamed on Cuba to justify an invasion
check.why: The memo proposed staging incidents that would look like Cuban attacks.

lessons.title: Rejected, Then Released
lessons.mainIdea: Kennedy rejected the use of U.S. military force in March 1962, and the Northwoods memo stayed secret until 1997.
reading: Northwoods was never carried out. On 16 March 1962, three days after the memo, military and civilian leaders met with President Kennedy. A memo about that meeting, written by General Edward Lansdale, records that the president said plainly that U.S. military force was not under discussion.

No record has been found of McNamara's own written reply to the memo. What is clear is that the civilian leaders did not approve the plan. Lemnitzer left the chairmanship later that year. This is how *civilian control of the military* is supposed to work: elected leaders, not generals, decide on war.

For thirty-five years the memo stayed classified. *Classified* means officially secret, open only to people with permission. After the 1991 film JFK stirred public interest, Congress passed a law in 1992 to release records about Kennedy's assassination. The Assassination Records Review Board reviewed millions of pages. In November 1997, it released the Northwoods memo.
The memo reached a wide audience in 2001, when journalist James Bamford wrote about it in his book Body of Secrets and the National Security Archive posted it online.

words.d: officially secret; open only to people with government permission
the principle that elected leaders, not generals, make the final decisions about military force
to officially remove the secret status from a document so the public may see it

look.title: The Meeting Three Days Later
look.text: At a White House meeting on 16 March 1962, the president told the group firmly that they were not discussing the use of U.S. military force against Cuba.
look.cite: Brig. Gen. Edward Lansdale, memorandum for the record of the meeting with the President, 16 March 1962, as released through the JFK Assassination Records Collection (paraphrase)
look.prompt: This memo is from the meeting itself. Why is it better evidence of Kennedy's answer than a memory told thirty years later?

check.q: What happened to the Northwoods plan?
choices: It was carried out after Kennedy died
It was rejected and never carried out
check.why: Kennedy said military force was not under discussion, and the plan was never carried out.

check.q: Which group released the Northwoods memo in November 1997?
choices: The Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI
check.why: The board created under the 1992 law released the memo in November 1997.

check.q: What does 'classified' mean?
choices: Officially secret, open only with permission
check.why: A classified document is officially secret; Northwoods stayed classified for thirty-five years.

lessons.title: How Secrets Are Tested
lessons.mainIdea: Real government secrets were proven by documents, and the same test of documents is how we judge claims about secrets that turn out to be false.
reading: Look back at the three secrets in this unit. MKUltra was proven by payment records and a Senate hearing. COINTELPRO was proven by stolen files, a FOIA lawsuit and a Senate report. Northwoods was proven by the memo itself. In every case, *documents* made the difference between suspicion and proof.

Real secrets leave traces. Money is paid, memos are written, and people remember and sometimes speak. Those traces can be found by reporters, courts, Congress and ordinary citizens. That is why real secrets were exposed, often years later.

The same test works in the other direction. When someone claims a huge secret plot, ask: what documents exist? Who made them, and when? Have they been checked? A claim that has no records after many years of searching is not proven. A document shown to be forged proves nothing except the forgery.

Northwoods also teaches a limit. It proves that a false flag plan was proposed in 1962 and rejected. It does not prove that any later event was staged. Each claim needs its own evidence. This is *evidence-based reasoning*: matching the size of a conclusion to the size of the proof.

words.d: reaching conclusions only as far as the evidence supports them
written or recorded materials, such as memos, receipts and reports, that can serve as evidence
a feeling or belief that something is wrong, without proof yet

look.title: Size the Claim to the Proof
look.text: Claim A: In 1962, the Joint Chiefs proposed staged attacks blamed on Cuba. Claim B: Because of Northwoods, we know a certain later disaster was staged by the government. Claim C: Some U.S. agencies have hidden wrongdoing that was later exposed by records.
look.prompt: Which claims does the evidence in this chapter support, and which one reaches too far? Explain using the idea of matching a conclusion to its proof.

check.q: What made the difference between suspicion and proof for MKUltra, COINTELPRO and Northwoods?
choices: Documents such as records, files and memos
check.why: In each case, documents turned suspicion into proof.

check.q: What does Northwoods prove, according to the reading?
choices: That every later disaster was staged
That Kennedy approved a false flag attack
That the Joint Chiefs never wrote such a plan
That a false flag plan was proposed in 1962 and rejected
check.why: Northwoods proves a plan was proposed and rejected; it does not prove any later event was staged.

check.q: What is evidence-based reasoning?
choices: Reaching conclusions only as far as the evidence supports
Believing any claim that sounds dramatic
check.why: Evidence-based reasoning matches the size of a conclusion to the size of the proof.

review.q: What did the Media, Pennsylvania, break-in in March 1971 reveal?
choices: FBI files that led to the discovery of COINTELPRO
review.why: The Media files included the word COINTELPRO and showed the FBI watching activists.

review.q: How did COINTELPRO differ from ordinary police work?
choices: It secretly tried to disrupt and discredit groups, not just investigate crimes
It was always approved by a judge
It was run by the Senate
review.why: COINTELPRO aimed to break up groups and damage reputations, often without any crime or court.

review.q: Which group was a COINTELPRO target?
review.why: The FBI added white hate groups, including the Klan, in 1964, alongside groups on the left.

review.q: What did lawsuits show about the FBI's role in the Hampton raid?
choices: The FBI had no knowledge of Hampton
An FBI informant had supplied a floor plan of the apartment
FBI agents carried out the raid themselves
The FBI warned Hampton before the raid
review.why: Records from Hampton v. Hanrahan showed informant William O'Neal gave the FBI a floor plan.

review.q: How are COINTELPRO and Operation Northwoods different?
choices: COINTELPRO was carried out against Americans; Northwoods was a proposal that was rejected
COINTELPRO was a CIA plan; Northwoods was an FBI plan
Both were carried out in Cuba
Both were revealed in the 1971 Media break-in
review.why: The FBI ran COINTELPRO from 1956 to 1971; Northwoods was a 1962 military proposal Kennedy's government rejected.

review.q: Why did the Northwoods memo stay hidden until 1997?
choices: It was classified until the Assassination Records Review Board released it
review.why: The memo was classified and released in November 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board.

review.q: Which statement is an example of evidence-based reasoning about Northwoods?
choices: Northwoods proves later disasters were staged
Northwoods proves nothing, because governments never keep secrets
Northwoods proves Kennedy wanted to invade Cuba with fake attacks
Northwoods proves a false flag plan was proposed in 1962 and rejected
review.why: That claim matches the evidence exactly; the others reach too far or ignore the document.

review.q: Which of these helped expose secrets in this chapter?
choices: A reporter's FOIA lawsuit and a Senate committee's report
review.why: Carl Stern's FOIA lawsuit and the Church Committee's report brought COINTELPRO's details to light.
